articles.title: Introduce age-appropriate awareness programmes for school students in academics over trafficking, commercial sexual exploitation: HC to government
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: High Court bench says that there should not be any delay in referring complaints relating to online sexual exploitation, intimate images or suspected child sexual abuse material to the competent police officer or cybercrime official

The Telangana High Court on Wednesday passed a slew of instructions to top officials of different wings of State government, including the Director General of Police, over rescue and rehabilitation of women and children rescued from trafficking and commercial sexual exploitation.

In one of the directions, the HC said ‘under no circumstances shall a Protective Home meant exclusively for victims be used as a place of penal detention or remand for perpetrators or organisers’. The bench of Acting Chief Justice Sam Koshy and Justice Narsing Rao Nandikonda gave these orders disposing of a writ petition filed by Prajwala, an NGO running a Protective Home, over rehabilitation of women and children rescued from traffickers and perpetrators of flesh trade.

The bench instructed the DGP to ensure coordination between different wings of police department over recruitment, grooming, coercion of women and children through social media, messaging applications, online advertisements, luring through placement offers. Police officers must be pro-active in identifying and preserving electronic records. “Any handling of devices or digital material shall preserve evidence related integrity and the privacy and dignity of victims, particularly children,”, the bench said.

There should not be any delay in referring complaints relating to online sexual exploitation, intimate images or suspected child sexual abuse material to the competent police officer or cybercrime official.
“Victims and families shall be informed of appropriate confidential reporting authorities and available protection,” the bench said.

The bench also directed the Education department officials to introduce age-appropriate awareness among children in each academic semester over recognising coercion, unsafe online contact, safe use of digital platforms and confidential access to teachers, counsellors and statutory reporting mechanisms. In colleges and universities, students should be explained about deceptive job and placement offers and exploitation through digital recruitment.

The bench instructed the Magistrates passing orders related to custody under section 17 of the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act-1956 to take precautions to prevent from placing genuine victims with the suspected exploiters in the same Preventive Home. It instructed the departments of Women and Child Development, Social Welfare, Health, Education and district administration to designate contact officers for coordination with the district Anti-Human Trafficking Units and District Legal Services Authorities.

articles.title: India’s Oct. crude import bill soars 87.5% to $19.5-bn amid West Asia tensions, volumes up 11%
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Updates
fullParagraphs: While higher petroleum product exports offer a partial natural hedge, sustained increases in crude and gas prices could intensify pressure on the country’s import bill.

India’s crude oil import bill surged 87.5% year-on-year (YoY) to $19.5 billion in October, as elevated international benchmark prices, fuelled by renewed tensions in West Asia, sharply increased procurement costs. The increase came alongside an 11% rise in import volumes.

The net import bill, calculated as imports of crude oil, petroleum products and natural gas less exports of petroleum products, rose 60% to $16 billion during the month, compared with $10 billion in October last year.
Higher export realisations from petroleum products, however, provided some cushion against the escalating import burden.

According to provisional data released by the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC), India imported 23.3 million metric tonnes (MMT) of crude oil in October, against 21 MMT in the corresponding month last year.
The expenditure on crude imports, meanwhile, climbed to $19.5 billion from $10.4 billion, reflecting the disproportionate impact of higher international prices on the country’s energy import bill.

The Indian crude oil basket averaged $119.91 per barrel in October, compared with $124.77 per barrel for Brent crude. In September, the Indian basket had averaged $116.09 per barrel, while Brent stood at $116.77 per barrel.

The sustained increase in benchmark prices, amid continuing geopolitical uncertainties in West Asia, has left India exposed to higher energy procurement costs, given its dependence on imported crude oil.
The impact of the rising crude import bill was partly offset by stronger earnings from petroleum product exports.
India’s petroleum product exports increased 5.9% in volume terms to 5.4 MMT in October. However, export revenues surged approximately 91% to $6.3 billion.
The increase in export earnings provided an important buffer against the higher cost of crude procurement.

Meanwhile, India’s liquefied natural gas (LNG) imports declined approximately 7% to 3,014 million standard cubic metres (MMSCM) during October. Despite the decline in volumes, the import bill increased 8.33%, pointing to the persistence of price pressures in the international gas market.

articles.title: Democrats nominate Hakeem Jeffries for next U.S. House speaker
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: Despite some opposition, Jeffries is expected to be elected speaker, a powerful position that puts him second in line to the Presidency, when the new Congress ‌convenes in early January

Democrats elected this month to the U.S. House ‌of Representatives nominated Hakeem Jeffries on Wednesday (November 18, 2026) to lead them in the next Congress, putting him ‌on the precipice of becoming the nation's first ‌Black ⁠House speaker.
The incoming House Democratic Caucus nominated Mr. Jeffries ⁠in a closed-door, secret-ballot vote.
Mr. Jeffries won 251 votes with 11 Democrats opposing him.

Many incoming progressives declined to say whether they would back Mr. ​Jeffries after the November ‌3 midterm elections, with several saying they wanted a leader who would support a bold agenda to pass populist policies that candidates campaigned on.
A group of seven ‌incoming House progressives said in a joint statement ​that they voted against Mr. Jeffries because they're still working to secure commitments from the New ⁠York Democrat.

"While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the ‌direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership," they said. "Those conversations are ongoing."

Despite some opposition, Mr. Jeffries is expected to be elected speaker, a powerful position that puts him second in line to the Presidency, when the new Congress ‌convenes in early January. The speaker election requires 218 votes on ​the House floor. Democrats will have a majority of at least 257 seats. Several competitive races ⁠remain uncalled.

House Republicans last week nominated Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan ⁠to lead their conference in January. Mr. Jordan won the post over Majority Leader Steve Scalise ‌after Speaker Mike Johnson said he would not seek to lead Republicans in the minority.

🎯 Exam Relevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics

Despite some opposition, Jeffries is expected to be elected speaker, a powerful position that puts him second in line to the Presidency, when the new Congress ‌convenes in early January

Democrats elected this month to the U.S. House ‌of Representatives nominated Hakeem Jeffries on Wednesday (November 18, 2026) to lead them in the next Congress, putting him ‌on the precipice of becoming the nation's first ‌Black ⁠House speaker.

The incoming House Democratic Caucus nominated Mr. Jeffries ⁠in a closed-door, secret-ballot vote.

Mr. Jeffries won 251 votes with 11 Democrats opposing him.

Many incoming progressives declined to say whether they would back Mr. ​Jeffries after the November ‌3 midterm elections, with several saying they wanted a leader who would support a bold agenda to pass populist policies that candidates campaigned on.

A group of seven ‌incoming House progressives said in a joint statement ​that they voted against Mr. Jeffries because they're still working to secure commitments from the New ⁠York Democrat.

"While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the ‌direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership," they said. "Those conversations are ongoing."

Despite some opposition, Mr. Jeffries is expected to be elected speaker, a powerful position that puts him second in line to the Presidency, when the new Congress ‌convenes in early January. The speaker election requires 218 votes on ​the House floor. Democrats will have a majority of at least 257 seats. Several competitive races ⁠remain uncalled.

House Republicans last week nominated Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan ⁠to lead their conference in January. Mr. Jordan won the post over Majority Leader Steve Scalise ‌after Speaker Mike Johnson said he would not seek to lead Republicans in the minority.

articles.title: Saudis prepare for Houthi war to last well into 2027
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: Saudi and Yemeni forces are ​now reorganising, with plans to protect Aden from the Houthi advances and potentially shift their offensive to eastern fronts where they have made some advances or have at least held their lines

Saudi Arabia is preparing for war against Yemen's Houthis to stretch well into next year, doubling down despite setbacks on the battlefield in Yemen ​and attacks disrupting life at home, said two Western officials briefed by Saudis on the plans.

The renewed conflict has become the most active front in ‌the wider Iran war, killing and wounding thousands and displacing hundreds of thousands in Yemen while derailing ​Saudi Arabia's efforts to draw in non-oil investment and host global events.
Public messaging around the war has also ⁠slowly shifted in the kingdom, with greater acknowledgement of its impacts.

Saudi officials now foresee the campaign stretching on for up to six months, aiming to see gains on the ground by the kingdom's Yemeni allies before any negotiations with the Houthis, according to Western officials, who spoke on condition ‌of anonymity to discuss non-public conversations with Saudi counterparts.
A third source familiar with the Saudi plans confirmed the accounts. All three said a deal to end the wider Iran war could see the Yemen conflict draw down.

The ‌third source also said Riyadh believes that U.S. offensive support for Saudi operations in Yemen, which President Donald Trump's administration has ‌so ⁠far withheld, could help change the tide of the conflict, potentially allowing Saudi-backed forces to make the gains ⁠they want within weeks.
A Saudi Foreign Ministry official declined to comment on the views of Saudi officials as described by the Western officials.

Saudi Arabia first entered the Yemen conflict in 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition to try to restore Yemen's government to power after the Houthis seized the ​capital Sanaa and much of the country. They fought to ‌a bloody stalemate and in 2022 reached a ceasefire that lasted until summer this year.

Since fighting restarted, the Houthis have seized the Red Sea coast and strategic Bab el-Mandeb strait from Saudi-backed forces, and encircled the city of Taiz in highlands above the government's temporary capital Aden on the southern coast.
Yemeni government forces mounted a counterattack last month, recapturing territory around the ‌strait, but withdrew over the past weekend to protect Aden in a major setback.

Saudi and Yemeni forces are ​now reorganising, with plans to protect Aden from the Houthi advances and potentially shift their offensive to eastern fronts where they have made some advances or have at least held their lines, according to one of the ⁠Western officials.

Saudi Arabia announced on Monday (November 16, 2026) it had replaced the commander overseeing the Saudi-led coalition. Yemen's government is also expected to reshuffle its military leadership, according to two people familiar with its plans.

articles.title: Ethiopia, Eritrea amass forces along border, heightening war fears: Sources
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: The fighting in Tigray has stoked fears of a ​wider conflagration in the Horn of Africa, with Ethiopia’s government also accusing Sudan, which is in the midst of its own civil war, and Egypt of backing the rebels; Eritrea, Sudan, Egypt ⁠all deny doing so

Ethiopia and Eritrea have amassed forces along their shared border, conflict monitors and people tied to militias in northern Ethiopia's Tigray ‌region said, fuelling fears of outright war between the historical rivals.

The build-up along the border has brought ​the two armies within striking distance of each other, according to the conflict monitors ACLED and the International ⁠Crisis Group, a person close to a pro-Ethiopian government militia in Tigray, and another person close to anti-government rebels there.

Reuters could not independently confirm reports of skirmishes between Ethiopian and Eritrean forces along the border. ACLED and a person close to the rebels said the ‌two sides had clashed in recent days, which would be their first direct armed exchanges in over a month, but the person close to the pro-Ethiopian government militia disputed this.

Reached for comment, Eritrean Information ‌Minister Yemane Gebremeskel decried "propaganda" from Ethiopia's ruling party about developments near the border but did not directly address reports about ‌military ⁠build-ups or clashes.
Spokespeople for the Ethiopian government did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Diplomats and ⁠experts have warned of possible conflict between Ethiopia and Eritrea since fighting broke out in September between Ethiopia’s federal government and rebels in Tigray, which borders Eritrea.

Witnesses and Ethiopia's government said Eritrean forces crossed into Tigray in early October in support ​of the rebels. ACLED reported at the time ‌that drone strikes it believed were carried out by Ethiopia’s military had targeted the Eritrean troops. Ethiopia has not commented on the strikes.

Eritrea has denied any incursion into Ethiopia and accused Addis Ababa of seeking a pretext to invade its smaller neighbour, which was an Ethiopian province for three decades before gaining independence in 1993. They are now separated ‌by a border stretching more than 1,000 km (620 miles).

The fighting in Tigray has stoked fears of a ​wider conflagration in the Horn of Africa, with Ethiopia’s government also accusing Sudan, which is in the midst of its own civil war, and Egypt of backing the rebels. Eritrea, Sudan, and Egypt ⁠all deny doing so.

Ethiopia and Eritrea fought a border war from 1998 to 2000 that killed tens of thousands of people. The conflict was prompted by a dispute over the border town of Badme, which a UN boundary commission later found fell within Eritrean ‌territory.

ACLED said in a statement late on Tuesday (November 17, 2026) that artillery shelling and armed clashes have occurred near Badme since last week as Ethiopia’s military moved to clear Tigrayan rebels from near the border.

It said that on November 12, Ethiopian drones targeted likely Eritrean positions around Badme and that Eritrean forces fired artillery toward Ethiopian positions. The next day, the two armies clashed on the Ethiopian side of the border, ACLED said.

articles.title: U.S.-Saudi nuclear agreement 'satisfactory': IAEA
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: According to the accord, the IAEA "will be provided with information about, and access to any sites for conversion, enrichment, fuel fabrication and reprocessing" in Saudi Arabia, Grossi said
UN nuclear watchdog head Rafael Grossi on Wednesday (November 18, 2026) welcomed a deal between the United States and Saudi Arabia on equipping the kingdom with a civilian nuclear programme.
The deal announced in July has provoked questions about the risks of nuclear proliferation.
"It's a very satisfactory outcome that we have with this agreement," Mr. Grossi told reporters after opening an International Atomic Energy Agency board of governors' meeting.
Once nuclear power development gets under way in Saudi Arabia, "we will be there," he added.

In his opening statement, Mr. Grossi told the board that the United States and Saudi Arabia in October requested the IAEA "to take the necessary steps to implement safeguards and verification measures" for their agreement.
According to the accord, the IAEA "will be provided with information about, and access to any sites for conversion, enrichment, fuel fabrication and reprocessing" in Saudi Arabia, Mr. Grossi said.
"I welcome the open, transparent approach and engagement of both governments with member states and the secretariat on this matter," he added.
Mr. Grossi told reporters the agreement was "fully aligned with the legal framework that we have at the IAEA".
He added Saudi Arabia had also agreed to "additional verification measures on a voluntary basis".
U.S. media have reported the agreement would allow Washington to export technology without the usual safeguards preventing future military use.
U.S. President Donald Trump said, just after the agreement was signed in July, that it depended on Saudi Arabia recognising Israel.

articles.title: India sitting on 'economic disaster': Rahul Gandhi at Columbia University
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: At Columbia University, Congress leader questions fairness of electoral process, speaks on manufacturing decline; links U.S. midterm setback to erosion of American power

Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi said the country’s economic model ceased to deliver results nearly a decade ago, leaving it with a deepening employment crisis and a weakened manufacturing base.

Speaking at a fireside chat at Columbia University on Tuesday (November 17, 2026), moderated by New York Times journalist Lydia Polgreen, Mr. Gandhi said India is sitting on an “economic disaster” that could become far more serious if the country continued on its present course.
“The blunt thing is that India is sitting on an economic disaster. That’s the reality of it,” he said.

“One can brush it aside, the media can brush it aside. But India has got a massive unemployment problem. India’s got a massive problem with its education system. And these are things you cannot get away from,” he added.

Mr. Gandhi identified small and medium businesses, agriculture and manufacturing as the backbone and principal engines of job creation, arguing that the services sector could not absorb India’s expanding workforce.

“The spine of the economy is small and medium business, which is the job creation engine, and agriculture. That is fundamental in India and required. The spine of the economy has been broken,” he said.

The Opposition leader said India could not achieve sustainable economic development without rebuilding its manufacturing capabilities. “We cannot survive successfully without manufacturing, it just cannot be done,” he said.
Mr. Gandhi alleged that economic growth was concentrated in a few large business groups while smaller enterprises were struggling.

“Why is there no private investment in India? Why are the only people who are growing in India, businesses that are growing in India called Adani and Ambani? Why is Tata literally being taken over by Mr. [Gautam] Adani?” he asked.

Mr. Gandhi placed the recent student-led Gen Z protests alongside resistance movements by Adivasis, Dalits and farmers against what he called the growing concentration of political and economic power in the last decade. He said the student-led protests showed that fear of “coercive power of the State” didn’t work.

“There’s a massive concentration of wealth taking place in India, and huge disenfranchisement of people. Vote is just one element of it,” he said, alleging that tribal land was being taken without consultation and that minorities, Dalits and farmers were facing growing marginalisation.

Referring to youth unemployment and economic difficulties in the U.S. and European countries, including Germany and Britain, Mr. Gandhi argued their economic challenges are serious and India’s relatively lower costs offer resilience, he said.

articles.title: UN Sustainable Development Goals group for science, technology rejigged
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: The group has been constituted even as the international community ramps up efforts to achieve the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development

The United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has reconstituted a 10-member group that works on promoting science, technology and innovation toward achieving its Sustainable Development Goals. The lone Indian in this group is former biologist and former Council of Scientific and Industrial Research CSIR Director General, Shekhar Mande, who is also currently President, Indian National Science Academy.
The group has been constituted even as the international community ramps up efforts to achieve the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, while preparing for the 2027 SDG Summit.

“The group comprises distinguished experts from diverse geographic and disciplinary backgrounds from both developing and developed countries. Each member, recognised for their international excellence in science or technology, brings a wealth of experience and insight from civil society, the private sector, and the scientific community, underscoring the inclusive and comprehensive approach the UN is taking towards sustainable development,” an accompanying press statement noted.

The other members of the group are Marian Dorcas Quain (Ghana), Deputy Director-General of CSIR Ghana; Giorgio Rossi (Italy), Vice-President of Elettra-Sincrotrone Trieste; Magnus Andersson (Sweden), Associate Professor at Malmö University; Mônica Tejo Cavalcanti (Brazil), Professor at the Federal University of Campina Grande; Evgeniya Dmitrieva (Russia), Member of the Civic Chamber of the Russian Federation; Motoko Kotani (Japan), Executive Director of Science at RIKEN; Jin Li (China), President of Fudan University; Madin Maseeh (Maldives), President of the Maldives Space Research Organisation; and Rita Orji (Nigeria), Canada Research Chair in Persuasive Technology at Dalhousie University.
Professor Mande is also President of Vijnana Bharti, which, along with the Ministry of Science and Technology is gearing up to host the India International Science Festival in Pune in December.

Announcing this on Wednesday (November 18, 2026), Union Minister of Science Jitendra Singh said at a press briefing that the government had taken a conscious decision to replace “scattered, repetitive gatherings”, including the erstwhile Indian Science Congress, with two flagship national events carrying distinct identities.

While the Emerging Science, Technology and Innovation Conclave in October saw 13 Ministries and Nobel Laureates, and was an academic-driven conclave exploring frontier themes, the India International Science Festival (IISF) brought a “festive, public-facing character with international resonance”. By rotating the venue to different regions, after Chandigarh, Hyderabad, Goa and Delhi, bringing IISF for the first time to Pune leverages the western hub’s vibrant academic, research, and industrial ecosystem.

articles.title: Bangladesh deploys paramilitary as unrest grows over Hasina's return
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: Police have recorded dozens of crude bomb blasts and incidents of vehicles ​being torched in at least ‌28 districts over the last 10 days, with several police personnel and civilians injured, local media has reported

Bangladesh ‌stepped up security and deployed hundreds of paramilitary troops nationwide on Wednesday (November 18, 2026) ​as the planned return of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina has ⁠sparked clashes, bomb blasts, and arson attacks blamed on supporters of her banned party.

Ms. Hasina, who has lived in exile in neighbouring India since she fled Dhaka following violent protests demanding ‌her resignation in August 2024, has requested a new passport and identity card, saying she plans to return in December.
But the government ‌has so far rejected her request, leading to members and supporters of ‌her ⁠Awami League party taking to the streets in protest.
Last week, the party ⁠announced a week-long programme of protests and rallies to mobilise support for Ms. Hasina's return, culminating in a nationwide lockdown on November 19.

Police have recorded dozens of crude bomb blasts and incidents of vehicles ​being torched in at least ‌28 districts over the last 10 days, with several police personnel and civilians injured, local media has reported.

Late on Tuesday (November 17, 2026), an activist of the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) was allegedly killed by unidentified people during a protest ‌near Ms. Hasina's home district of Gopalganj, police said.

On the same night, a ​crude bomb exploded outside the Dhaka residence of Cultural Affairs Minister Nitai Roy Chowdhury, and the house of a BNP lawmaker and ⁠shops belonging to BNP supporters in Gopalganj were set on fire, police added.
On Wednesday (November 18, 2026) morning, a bus company helper was burnt to death in the southern district ‌of Pirojpur after two buses were set on fire, authorities said.

Tuesday (November 17, 2026) marked the day on which Ms. Hasina was sentenced to death a year ago by a local court that found her guilty of ordering a deadly crackdown on the student-led uprising against her in 2024.

At least 37 Grameen Bank branches and offices have been targeted in arson attacks or attempted fires ‌since November 10, with 14 more attacked since midnight on Tuesday (November 17, 2026), the bank said.
The bank was ​founded by Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus, who led Bangladesh's interim government after Ms. Hasina's ouster and has faced hostility from Ms. Hasina's supporters.

Dhaka Metropolitan ⁠Police have arrested at least 71 members of banned organisations, including the Awami League ⁠and its affiliated outfits, in the last 24 hours, police spokesperson Niaz Mehedi said.

articles.title: Trump's Board of Peace faults Israel, Hamas for failure to end Gaza war
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: While the ceasefire has halted major fighting, the wider plan, which calls for Hamas ⁠to disarm, Israeli troops to withdraw and reconstruction to begin, has effectively stalled since soon after it came into effect last year

The body overseeing U.S. President Donald Trump's plan to end the Gaza ‌war accused both Israel and Hamas of failing to meet their commitments to end hostilities, leaving ​the population of Gaza in dire conditions and the ceasefire in danger of collapse.

The 12-page Board ⁠of Peace report, seen by Reuters , is the body's second to the United Nations Security Council since the U.S.-backed ceasefire came into effect 13 months ago. It offers a sobering assessment of progress made since then.
The Board, established and headed by Mr. Trump, is expected ‌to present the report's findings to a meeting of the council in New York at the end of November.

"The distance between what has been agreed and what is happening on the ground nonetheless remains ‌the principal risk to the process," the report said, warning that "a ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be ‌sustained ⁠indefinitely."

While the ceasefire has halted major fighting, the wider plan, which calls for Hamas ⁠to disarm, Israeli troops to withdraw and reconstruction to begin, has effectively stalled since soon after it came into effect last year.

Hamas agreed in July to a Board of Peace roadmap to surrender its weapons and transfer governance of Gaza to a civilian transitional authority, but Israel rejected ​the roadmap, saying it will not withdraw until Hamas ‌is dismantled.
Israel has carried out near-daily strikes on Gaza, while the report said Hamas fighters have also continued attacks on Israeli troops.
"Every day that Israel continues strikes against Hamas targets, it delays putting Hamas' agreement to the roadmap to the test," the report said.
"Meanwhile, Hamas militant activity continues, the commitment to cease all military activities has not ‌been met in full by the parties, and the population faces another winter in tents and rubble."

Senior Hamas ​official Basem Naim dismissed the report as "pure disinformation", accusing the Board of Peace of providing cover to Israel to evade its commitments under the plan to end the war and to ⁠continue its aggression in Gaza.
The office of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and a spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Gaza's population of more than 2 million Palestinians lives confined to around a third of ‌the coastal territory, mostly in makeshift tents and damaged buildings, under the control of Hamas fighters. Israel occupies two-thirds of Gaza that has been largely razed and depopulated.

articles.title: How AI could reshape global growth and productivity
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Updates
fullParagraphs: A key expected impact of AI is an unprecedented rise in labour productivity, as its success as a technological revolution is premised on such an increase; what remains to be seen is how pervasive its impact will be across different sectors of the economy

Many have likened the artificial intelligence (AI) phenomenon to the inventions of the steam engine or internal combustion engine in the 18th and 19th centuries, respectively. Only time can tell whether AI is epochal of that kind. In this two-part piece, we discuss the possible impact it may have on the global economy as a whole.

A key impact of AI is considered to be an unprecedented rise in labour productivity. In fact, if there is one purpose AI is supposed to serve, it is enhancing labour productivity multifold. Since labour productivity is a key variable in this puzzle, consider what it constitutes of (Box 1) . It is a ratio of output and workers employed. Now this ratio can rise in three different ways — a rise in output for a given number of workers employed (rise in the numerator); a loss of jobs which leads to a fall in the denominator; more jobs are created, but the output rises faster than the jobs (while both the numerator and the denominator are rising, the numerator rises faster than the denominator).

Now this ratio can rise in three different ways — a rise in output for a given number of workers employed (rise in the numerator); a loss of jobs which leads to a fall in the denominator; more jobs are created, but the output rises faster than the jobs (while both the numerator and the denominator are rising, the numerator rises faster than the denominator).

At the same time, the Supreme Court has increasingly restricted capital punishment and research has failed to find evidence of additional deterrence over life imprisonment . India’s distinction between judicial executions and extrajudicial killings is legally valid but its further claim that due process protects people facing execution is less so. While India last executed convicts in 2020, for the Delhi gang-rape and murder, Parliament expanded the number of capital offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita — a form of penal populism that projects the political attractiveness of the state’s response to public outrage, especially in cases of sexual violence, without addressing the poor policing and low conviction rates that actually undermine deterrence . The country had 574 people on death row on December 31, 2025, the highest since 2016, thanks to trial court rulings, challenging claims about judicial safeguards in practice. The report of the 2015 Law Commission headed by Justice A.P. Shah said the death penalty “fails to achieve any constitutionally valid penological goals” and recommended abolishing it for all crimes except terrorism and waging war.
